catalog_quote: Some important features like vowel length and tone will be examined in this chapter. Mmɛn like Aghem or many other Western grassfields languages is a tone language. It is a language in which both segmental and pitch phonemes, otherwise known as tones, go into the composition of words. It is known that in tone languages, words could either be distinguished on the basis of segments or/and tones; Mmɛn is no exception. The tones attested in the language are in some cases contrastive. [p. 67] ... III.2. Tones. There are principally five tones in Mmɛn namely - the high tone [ ´] - the mid tone [ ¯] - the low tone [ `] - the rising tone [ ˇ] - the falling tone [ ˆ] [p. 67] ... III.2.1. Phonemic tone contrast: Each syllable carries one of the five contrastive tones above mentioned occurring in the language. The falling and the rising tones occur less frequently than either of the other three tones while the high and low are much more attested than all. If one could count the frequency of occurrence, one might say these two tones (the rising and the falling tones) are attested in barely one per cent of the total vocabulary. Although rare, they can convey different meaning when attested in a syllable. [p. 68] ... Five suprasegmental phonemes (tones), three of which are level and two contour come up to confirm Mmɛn as a tone language. [p. 77]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Mmen is described as a tone language: every syllable bears one of five contrastive tones (H, M, L, rising LH, falling HL); the suprasegmental chapter treats vowel length and tone only and makes no statement about word stress or accent. No source examined (Agha 1987; Bangha 2003; Möller 2012; Nilsson 2013; Chiatoh 1993) mentions stress at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: rising and falling tones are rare (about one percent of vocabulary, p. 68) and the rising tone is in some cases non-contrastive (p. 69); Möller 2012:6 notes surface M whose contrastiveness needs more research.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level: tones assigned per syllable, described from words cited in isolation (Agha 1987) and in a 'same X' frame (Möller 2012). Nilsson 2013 stresses that her tone marks are surface pitches of citation forms, not underlying tones.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Mmen of Bafumen (Bafmen/Bafmeng), Fungom Subdivision, Menchum Division, NW Cameroon — Glottolog language-level mmen1238 (ISO bfm), Center/Central Ring Grassfields Bantu; Agha 1987 calls it a 'Western grassfields' language. No dialect is singled out; Troyer et al. 1995 (not downloaded) is the dialect survey.

sources.note: §1.3.4 'Mmen language structure' (p. 10) summarises Björkestedt 2011a:44: 27 consonants, 9 vowels, nine phonetic pitches on isolated syllables (H, M, L, HL, HM, ML, LM, MH, low-falling); 'm' can be tone-bearing as the cl. 6a prefix. tone.quote: As in the Ring and Momo sub-groups of Western Grassfields Bantu generally, noun class prefixes (NPx) in Central Ring languages have high tone underlyingly. ... In isolation, the high tone in these noun prefixes is generally lowered to mid, as is shown in Table 3, while the low tone in Babanki noun prefixes is maintained as such ... which is obvious in nouns such as ‘tree’. In all of CR, it bears a HL falling contour tone in the root, while in Babanki it is low throughout.
